title: The Fine Print on Evaluation and Diagnosis
description: Evaluation rules most parents never hear about: you can ask for one, the 60 day clock, no single test, and why a diagnosis is not the same as eligibility.
summary: You can ask for an evaluation, the 60 day clock, no single test, and diagnosis versus eligibility.
short_answer: A parent can ask the school for an evaluation, and the school generally has 60 days after consent (or the state's own deadline) to finish. The school cannot rely on a single test, the parent is part of the eligibility decision, and a doctor's diagnosis is not the same as eligibility for services. Under three, a referral for a suspected disability is enough to start Early Intervention.
h1: The Fine Print on Evaluation and Diagnosis
intro: The evaluation is where it all starts, and it is the step with the most myths. Here is what the federal rules actually say, with the exact sentences so you can point to them, and what to say.

sections.h2: You Can Ask for the Evaluation Yourself
sections.html:
You do not have to wait for the school to decide your child needs one. A parent can start the process, and you do not need a doctor's letter to ask.

The rule says: “either a parent of a child or a public agency may initiate a request for an initial evaluation to determine if the child is a child with a disability” (34 CFR 300.301)

Put the request in writing and keep a copy. The school needs your consent before it evaluates, which is one of the “two yeses” on the Be in Charge page.

Say: “I am requesting an initial evaluation of my child for special education. Please send me the consent form and tell me the timeline.”

After you give consent, the school has a deadline. Many states set their own, so ask what yours is.

The rule says: “Must be conducted within 60 days of receiving parental consent for the evaluation” (34 CFR 300.301)

The rule says: “If the State establishes a timeframe within which the evaluation must be conducted, within that timeframe” (34 CFR 300.301)

The clock does not apply if a parent repeatedly fails or refuses to bring the child in, or if the child moves to a different school district partway through. Write down the date you signed consent.

sections.h2: It Cannot Come Down to One Test
sections.html:
A single score or a single observation is not supposed to decide your child's future. The rule says the school has to pull information from several places, and you are one of them.

The rule says: “Not use any single measure or assessment as the sole criterion for determining whether a child is a child with a disability” (34 CFR 300.304)

The rule says: “including information provided by the parent” (34 CFR 300.304)

Bring what you know: reports from the doctor or therapists, your own notes, examples from home. Roy's Diagnosis page covers the first 90 days after a diagnosis.

sections.h2: You Are Part of the Decision
sections.html:
When the testing is done, the school does not decide alone.

The rule says: “A group of qualified professionals and the parent of the child determines whether the child is a child with a disability” (34 CFR 300.306)

And you are entitled to the paperwork.

The rule says: “The public agency provides a copy of the evaluation report and the documentation of determination of eligibility at no cost to the parent” (34 CFR 300.306)

If you disagree with the results, the school fine print explains the independent evaluation.

sections.h2: A Diagnosis Is Not the Same as Eligibility
sections.html:
A diagnosis from a doctor and eligibility for school services are two different things. In the school rule, the child has to be evaluated by the school's process and has to need special education because of the disability.

The rule says: “and who, by reason thereof, needs special education and related services” (34 CFR 300.8)

So a child with a diagnosis can still be turned down if the school finds they do not need special education, and a doctor's diagnosis is one piece of information the school has to consider rather than the whole answer. For autism, the school definition describes a developmental disability affecting communication and social interaction.

The rule says: “Autism means a developmental disability significantly affecting verbal and nonverbal communication and social interaction, generally evident before age three” (34 CFR 300.8)

If the answer is no and you disagree, ask for the reasons in writing. The letters page has a short request.

sections.h2: Under Three, Suspecting a Disability Is Enough
sections.html:
For Early Intervention the trigger is not a diagnosis. It is a referral and a suspicion.

The rule says: “each child under the age of three who is referred for evaluation or early intervention services under this part and suspected of having a disability” (34 CFR 303.321)

That child is supposed to get a timely, multidisciplinary evaluation, with your consent. The Early Intervention fine print has the 45 day clock and what to say.

sections.h2: A Way to Ask That Works
sections.html: Write down what you are seeing, the date, and what you are asking for. A short, kind, specific note is easier for a busy person to say yes to. If the answer is no, the disagree-in-writing guide shows what comes next. Your state's rules add to these, so check Your State.

checked: Every quoted sentence on this page was checked, word for word, against the text of 34 CFR 300.8, 300.301, 300.304, 300.306 and 303.321 at ecfr.gov. Your state may add rules of its own.
